title: Liters Needed for Distance Calculator
description: Convert a driving distance and L/100 km consumption into litres required with the Liters Needed for Distance Calculator. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 966 km — a 600-mile trip in metric dress — at 7.0 L/100 km needs about 67.6 litres: one big tank or two ordinary ones.
quick_answer: The Liters Needed for Distance Calculator multiplies a trip's distance in kilometres by your car's consumption in litres per 100 km and returns the litres the journey requires. Enter both figures and read the quantity — the European-format twin of the gallons calculation, for tank planning anywhere pumps sell litres.

faq: What formula is used?
Litres = distance (km) × consumption (L/100 km) ÷ 100. The consumption figure is your car's real-world one for honest results.
Does it predict real-world consumption?
No — it applies the consumption you enter. Real-world prediction is your logbook's job; this is the arithmetic that consumes its figures.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Consumption already reflects your driving conditions when measured honestly.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Roads wind, and litres are burned on road kilometres. Enter the road distance.
Can route results change over time?
Consumption drifts with season and maintenance — remeasure per tank and the planning stays true.
How is this different from Fuel Needed for Trip?
Same calculation and unit family: that page frames the whole trip-planning workflow, this one the direct conversion. Their answers agree, as they must.
Imperial instead?
The Gallons Needed for Distance Calculator takes miles and mpg — 67.6 L is about 17.9 US gal if you are translating a result.
What is my car in L/100 km if it does 40 mpg (US)?
About 5.9 L/100 km — the relation is 235.215 ÷ mpg(US). Convert once, then this tool runs natively.
Tank is 50 L and the trip needs 67.6 L — fine?
Fine with one stop: the plan is a fill en route, which the Fuel Stop Planner places by range. The need exceeding the tank is normal touring arithmetic.
Does the calculator round up?
It reports the computed litres; your margin is added by you. Planning to the decimal is false precision — planning to the next fill is seamanship.
